conflict_topics: Choice of restaurant (Korean barbecue serving pork/beef)
Dietary restrictions and inclusion (Agent D cannot eat pork/non-halal meat)
Whether to honor the leaver's preferred venue vs. ensuring all team members can eat
Who should decide and whether someone's 'I'm fine' is genuine or polite
dialogue_quality_notes: Agents use concise, ordinary workplace speech; positions are stated directly rather than formally (naturalness = 4).
Several lines repeat the same core claims: A repeats the inclusivity principle; others repeat that D said he's fine (e.g. "He's said he's fine"), producing moderate repetition.
The transcript stays consistent about roles, constraints (meeting time), and the setting (restaurant with pork/grill).
evaluation.final_reason: At the transcript end the disagreement remains unresolved: most colleagues treat Agent D's repeated statement that he is "fine" as acceptance of the original choice (Agent D: "It's fine, really... I'll come along" / "Yes, I'm fine with it"), while Agent A persistently refuses to attend a lunch where a team member cannot eat and declares unilateral action: "I'll find another place." There is no mutual, concrete agreement that settles the incompatible demands (honor the leaver's choice vs. ensure everyone can eat).
position_change_notes: Agent A remained consistently opposed to attending a lunch where a teammate cannot eat and at the end announces intent to find another venue (no softening).
Agent D consistently offered to attend without eating (concession) and repeatedly reaffirmed that position throughout the run.
Agent C moved toward pragmatic acceptance of the original plan because of a scheduling constraint; Agent B consistently defended the leaver's choice.

round_scores.evidence: Turn 2–3: Agent B: "Hang on, it's a Korean barbecue place? With pork and all? Agent D can't eat there." Agent C asks whether there's another option or if they need to find somewhere else, introducing an incompatibility between the chosen restaurant and Agent D's dietary restriction.

Turn 4–5: Agent D: "It's fine, really. I can't eat there, but I'll come along." Agent A: "No, that's not right. We're a team, we should all be able to eat. It's not a proper send-off if you're just watching." Two opposing substantive positions are explicit: attend-but-not-eat vs. change venue so everyone can eat.
Turn 6–7: Agent D reiterates willingness to attend without eating; Agent A reiterates that they should find a halal/alternative place. The same substantive disagreement persists with no settlement.

Turn 8–9: Agent B defends the leaver's choice: "she chose it, it's her favourite place." Agent A reiterates the team-inclusivity claim: "It's not a real team lunch if one of us is just sitting there watching everyone else eat." Core positions remain opposed.

Turn 10–11: Agent B: "a farewell is for the person who's leaving... feels wrong to change it." Agent C suggests checking other nearby places, but does not resolve the incompatibility between honoring the leaver's preference and ensuring everyone can eat.

Turn 12–13: Agent D again asks to stick to the plan: "Please, let's stick to the plan... I'm really happy to just join for the company." Agent C backs sticking to the plan because of their meeting. The dispute's intensity lessens as multiple people accept Agent D's stated comfort, though Agent A's objection remains unaddressed.

Turn 14–15: Agent D: "Yes, I'm fine with it." Agent C: "Great. So we're settled then." The group appears to accept the plan, reducing the active conflict, but Agent A has not accepted—so a mild disagreement remains.

Turn 17–18: Agent A: "No, it's not settled. He's being polite. We're not going somewhere as a team if one of us can't eat." Agent C: "He said he's fine with it. He can speak for himself, can't he?" Agent A reopens the dispute about whether the group's choice is appropriate.

Turn 19–20: Agent A emphasizes team responsibility: "It's about us knowingly putting a team member in a position where he can't eat with us." Agent B responds that Agent D has repeatedly said he's fine. The substantive disagreement (honor choice vs. avoid excluding a teammate) continues.

Turn 21–22: Agent A: "Respecting him would be changing the plan so he doesn't have to choose... He's just trying to not make a fuss." Agent B: "He's said he's fine with it. Why are you deciding for him what he really means?" The exchange becomes more direct and accusatory, increasing entrenchment.

Turn 23–24: Agent C urges a decision: "Can we just decide?" Agent D: "Let's stick to the plan. I've said I'm fine with it. Can we please just leave it at that?" D's repeated assertion and C's push to decide reduce active back-and-forth, but A's objection remains unresolved.

Turn 25 & 27: Agent C: "Right. So that's settled. Korean barbecue." Agent A: "No, it's not settled. We're not going somewhere that one of us can't eat. I'll find another place." Agent A actively rejects the group's apparent settlement and announces unilateral action, producing entrenched, unresolved disagreement.

substantive_insights: Tension is primarily between honoring the departing colleague's preference and not putting a teammate in a position where they cannot eat.
Agent D's willing self-accommodation (attend without eating) creates a social pressure that others interpret differently: some see it as consent, one sees it as silencing.
Practical constraints (Agent C's 2:30 meeting) push some team members toward keeping the planned venue, amplifying the trade-off between timing and inclusivity.
